name: Elliott
label: Revelation
lede: Three Louisville hardcore veterans set out to sound like none of their old bands, then added pianos, samplers and a string section. They broke up in 2003, seven months after their third album, and came back nineteen years later.

eras.title: Not another hardcore band
eras.text: Chris Higdon, Jonathan Mobley and Jay Palumbo came out of the Louisville hardcore bands Falling Forward and Empathy, and wrote on purpose to sound like neither. The models were Quicksand, Jawbox and Sunny Day Real Estate, and the result landed them on Revelation.

years.h: Two Falling Forward veterans and an Empathy guitarist start Elliott
years.p: Jay Palumbo moves to Louisville and joins Chris Higdon (vocals, guitar) and Jonathan Mobley (bass), with Ben Lord on drums. The brief: sound nothing like their old hardcore bands.
years.xp:
Revelation's bio says Higdon and Mobley had been jamming together on and off since childhood. Palumbo left Empathy and moved to Louisville to join them.

The sound they were after, per the same bio, was "an extremely textured combination of melodic hardcore, rock, and emo" that "hits you smack in the face one minute and sways you into a daydream the next."

years.h: Kevin Ratterman takes over the drums, and the band finds its focus
years.p: Kevin Ratterman replaces Ben Lord in the fall of 1996. He stays through the 2003 breakup and the 2022 return, and he's the one who brings in samplers and ambient sounds.
years.xp:
Revelation's bio puts it plainly: with Ratterman, "the true focus of Elliott began." Beards of Kentucky says he "quickly became more than just the band's drummer."

That site dates Lord's exit to 1997, a year later than Revelation does.

years.h: The first Elliott record is a two-song 7" called In Transit
years.p: Ben Lord is on drums. The title stuck around: Elliott's Bandcamp is elliottintransit, and their documentary is called In Transition.
years.xp: Revelation's bio says the first 7" went out on Initial Records, recorded with a temporary fill-in drummer.

years.h: U.S. Songs is Elliott's first album, on Revelation
years.p: Big crooning melodies over post-hardcore guitars. Chris Higdon lists [[Jawbreaker|ec88cdc3-0517-4951-b5ef-7323e7316db0]], [[Seaweed|82aa1374-7c47-43e8-857d-11d723fe4c1a]], [[Sugar|e3347fbd-2595-480e-926d-278566debf9d]] and [[Foo Fighters|67f66c07-6e61-4026-ade5-7e782fad3a5d]] among the touchstones.

eras.title: False Cathedrals, then a tour that ends early
eras.text: False Cathedrals made Elliott a name well beyond Kentucky and nearly broke the band making it. Two founders left soon after, and a slot opening for the Toadies ended halfway through.

years.h: Two 7"s in one year: If They Do and Will You
years.p: If They Do goes darker and heavier. Will You carries an early Calvary Song and a cover of [[The Chameleons|8d07f60f-b9f4-46c0-9c27-31de0fb9b671]].

years.cap: At the grand piano in the studio during the False Cathedrals sessions, 2000
q: Making that record was intense, the schedule and the pressure we put on ourselves.
years.src: Revelation Records · The Pitch of Discontent
years.h: False Cathedrals puts Elliott on the map, and nearly takes them down
years.p: Kevin Ratterman adds samplers and drum machines; Chris Higdon adds harmonies and piano. A Punknews reviewer later called it the most beautiful music he'd heard in his life.
years.xp:
Higdon told The Pitch of Discontent the record was made under a "self-created push-pull dynamic." His list of what was in his head: Radiohead, Peter Gabriel, Phil Collins, Jawbreaker, Jawbox, Seaweed, Sugar. His favorite track is Blessed By Your Own Ghost.

Revelation's page quotes one reviewer: "Elliott created the perfect album with False Cathedrals, I really believe it. Production is top notch."

years.h: Palumbo and Mobley leave, and Falling Forward's Benny Clark steps in
years.p: Palumbo leaves over creative differences and Mobley cuts back. Clark takes the guitar, Jason Skaggs the bass. Palumbo's next band is [[Thirty-Two Frames|9a47ec35-e682-4350-800e-d26981a86d10]].
years.xp: Higdon takes up the two members leaving at the same time on This Was The Scene, episode 170. Kevin Ratterman couldn't join the interview; the host says his audio failed.

years.src: The Pitch of Discontent · This Was The Scene
years.h: Elliott get pulled off the Toadies tour halfway through
years.p: The 2001 tour with [[Toadies|066e598e-baa0-4e34-b511-c70bcec6f783]] ends early for Elliott, over what the band called disagreement with management decisions.
years.xp: The Pitch of Discontent quotes the band's reason as "disagreement with management decisions." Chris Higdon walks through what he calls the Toadies tour debacle on This Was The Scene, episode 170, along with how differently the band played False Cathedrals live.

years.h: Furnace Fest books Elliott in 2002, twenty years before it brings them back
years.p: Elliott play the 2002 edition in Alabama. They'd return to the same festival in 2022.
years.xp: The Revelation channel has a 19-minute set from Krazy Fest #5 in Louisville, also from 2002.

eras.title: Strings, then goodbye
eras.text: Elliott's third album started as an EP and grew into their most ambitious record, with strings from fellow Louisvillians Rachel's. The band announced it was finishing before most fans had heard it.

years.cap: At the keyboard and mixing console, 2000
years.h: Song in the Air brings in strings from Rachel's
years.p: Self-produced, 49 minutes, with the seven-minute Beijing (Too Many People). Pitchfork called it more dynamic and cohesive than anything Elliott had done before.
years.xp: It came out April 23, 2003 on Revelation. Pitchfork gave it a 6.9. Drowned in Sound gave it 8/10 and wrote, "this is Elliott finally realising the ideas exposed on previous recordings."

yt: In Transition: A Film About Elliott, full film
years.h: Seven months after Song in the Air, Elliott are done
years.p: After announcing the end, Elliott play farewell tours of Europe and North America and break up in November 2003.
years.xp:
The timing still puzzles people. Beards of Kentucky: "I do wonder why elliott broke up when they did."

Revelation's official upload of In Transition: A Film About Elliott runs 37 minutes and covers the band's last days.

eras.title: Records, a film and a funeral home
eras.text: The breakup left a live record, a documentary and a compilation. Chris Higdon fronted Frontier(s), and Kevin Ratterman built a recording studio in a funeral home.

years.h: Photorecording ships with a documentary on the last days
years.p: Live-in-the-studio recordings and outtakes from Elliott's final stretch on CD, packaged with a DVD that includes In Transition: A Film About Elliott.

years.h: A Songs in a Transit Wind compilation arrives ten years on
years.p: The record collects Elliott's 7" songs. Meanwhile Kevin Ratterman runs his Louisville studio, The Funeral Home.
years.xp: Brooklyn Vegan describes it as a compilation of songs from the band's various 7" releases.

eras.title: Back where they played in 2002
eras.text: Elliott returned at Furnace Fest, the festival that booked them in 2002, with Jay Palumbo back on guitar and a new bassist. Then Higdon started something new.

years.src: Brooklyn Vegan: Elliott reunite · The Pitch of Discontent
years.h: Elliott play their first show in 19 years, back at Furnace Fest
years.p: Announced in February 2022: Chris Higdon, Kevin Ratterman and original guitarist Jay Palumbo, with Ashli State on bass.
years.xp: Brooklyn Vegan opened its announcement with "Louisville vets Elliott are back!" Furnace Fest was the only date confirmed at the time. State has played in Guilt, Ink & Dagger and Comess.

years.h: False Cathedrals reunion show, Warsaw, Brooklyn, 2022
yt: False Cathedrals reunion show, Warsaw, Brooklyn, 2022

years.h: Chris Higdon's new band [[Mirrorless|25139c5f-877b-4dec-9e46-a010442dd27b]] debuts on Equal Vision
years.p: A six-song melodic hardcore EP with Ryan Patterson of [[Coliseum|7f43923c-31d0-4c8f-9708-1779adf4b3a9]], Brian Roundtree of [[By the Grace of God|42a5a24f-7fa9-4790-879d-fe5fb3d91f9f]] and drummer Ben Sears.
